title: Front-End Web Engineering
description: A beginner-to-junior professional curriculum grounded in the web platform, accessible responsive implementation, JavaScript and browser reasoning, TypeScript, React, testing, deployment, and cross-functional delivery.

target.learner: Complete beginner with basic computer literacy only
target.professionalOutcome: Independently build, debug, test, optimize, and deploy responsive, accessible web interfaces from product requirements, visual designs, and API contracts under appropriate junior supervision.

phases.title: The Web Platform
phases.outcome: Build semantic, accessible, responsive interfaces with HTML and CSS while learning how browsers and development tools work.

phases.title: JavaScript in the Browser
phases.outcome: Use JavaScript, the DOM, browser storage, HTTP, and asynchronous APIs to build and debug interactive applications.

phases.title: Typed Professional Workflow
phases.outcome: Use Git, modern tooling, TypeScript, and automated tests in a maintainable frontend workflow.

phases.title: React Product Engineering
phases.outcome: Build accessible, routed, data-driven React applications with intentional state, component, and testing boundaries.

phases.title: Production and Professional Readiness
phases.outcome: Measure, secure, deploy, collaborate on, and present production-quality frontend applications and an independent capstone.

competencies.name: Trace a basic web request
competencies.description: Explain how a URL leads from a browser request to a server response and rendered page without confusing the browser with the server.

competencies.name: Create and inspect a local webpage
competencies.description: Create named HTML files in a deliberate folder, open them in a browser, and inspect source and rendered output with browser tools.

competencies.name: Choose semantic HTML elements
competencies.description: Select elements that express the meaning and relationship of content rather than choosing containers only for appearance.

competencies.name: Create navigable document structure
competencies.description: Organize headings, landmarks, links, lists, images, and metadata so people and user agents can understand the page.

competencies.name: Build an accessible native form
competencies.description: Use labels, suitable controls, groups, instructions, required states, and error feedback that remain understandable by keyboard and assistive technology users.

competencies.name: Represent tabular data semantically
competencies.description: Use tables only for related row-and-column data and provide headers and captions that expose relationships.

competencies.name: Reason about the CSS cascade
competencies.description: Use origin, importance, specificity, source order, and inheritance to explain why a declaration wins.

competencies.name: Control boxes and readable type
competencies.description: Apply box sizing, dimensions, spacing, borders, color, fonts, line height, and measure without breaking content.

competencies.name: Build one-dimensional layouts with Flexbox
competencies.description: Use axes, wrapping, alignment, growth, shrinkage, and basis to arrange interface groups.

competencies.name: Build two-dimensional layouts with Grid
competencies.description: Define tracks, gaps, placement, and responsive grids while choosing Grid or Flexbox according to the relationship.

competencies.name: Implement mobile-first responsive layouts
competencies.description: Begin from constrained content, add breakpoints when the layout needs them, and preserve priority and operability across viewports.

competencies.name: Deliver responsive images and touch-friendly controls
competencies.description: Use fluid media, suitable image sources, viewport configuration, and minimum interaction targets without distorting content.

competencies.name: Trace JavaScript execution with basic data
competencies.description: Predict how values, types, variables, expressions, and operators are evaluated in a short program.

competencies.name: Control program flow
competencies.description: Use conditionals and loops to express bounded decisions and repetition while avoiding accidental infinite work.

competencies.name: Design focused JavaScript functions
competencies.description: Define parameters, return values, and responsibilities so behavior can be reused and tested without relying on hidden global state.

competencies.name: Organize browser code with modules
competencies.description: Export and import named responsibilities while reasoning about local, function, block, and module scope.

competencies.name: Model frontend data with arrays and objects
competencies.description: Choose arrays for ordered collections and objects for named properties, then access, update, copy, destructure, and compare them deliberately.

competencies.name: Transform collections with array methods
competencies.description: Use map, filter, find, some, every, and reduce where their output matches the intended data transformation.

competencies.name: Manipulate the DOM safely
competencies.description: Select elements, create and remove nodes, update text, attributes, and classes, and avoid unsafe HTML insertion for untrusted content.

competencies.name: Design event-driven interactions
competencies.description: Handle events, default behavior, propagation, delegation, and small UI state transitions without duplicate or inaccessible controls.

competencies.name: Implement usable client-side form behavior
competencies.description: Read form data, validate rules, present field-specific feedback, preserve input after failure, and distinguish client validation from server authority.

competencies.name: Use browser storage deliberately
competencies.description: Store, parse, update, and remove non-sensitive local data while recognizing origin scope, string serialization, and privacy limits.

competencies.name: Interpret frontend HTTP exchanges
competencies.description: Read URLs, methods, status codes, headers, and JSON response shapes at the depth needed to collaborate from an API contract.

competencies.name: Coordinate asynchronous fetch flows
competencies.description: Use promises and async/await to fetch, parse, validate, cancel or ignore stale work, and surface loading, empty, success, and error states.

competencies.name: Diagnose frontend failures systematically
competencies.description: Reproduce a defect, reduce its scope, inspect evidence, form a falsifiable hypothesis, and verify the smallest repair.

competencies.name: Handle expected JavaScript failures
competencies.description: Use thrown errors and targeted try/catch boundaries while preserving useful messages and avoiding silent failure.

competencies.name: Architect a small vanilla web application
competencies.description: Separate data access, state, rendering, and interaction responsibilities while keeping the application explainable without a framework.

competencies.name: Deliver a resilient API-backed feature
competencies.description: Implement requirements across responsive, accessible, async, empty, error, persistence, and documentation concerns.

competencies.name: Manage source history with Git
competencies.description: Inspect working-tree state, stage intentional changes, write meaningful commits, branch, merge, pull, push, and resolve a basic conflict without discarding work.

competencies.name: Collaborate through GitHub pull requests
competencies.description: Publish a branch, explain its scope, review a diff, respond to feedback, and merge through a pull-request workflow.

competencies.name: Operate a Node and npm project
competencies.description: Explain Node’s tooling role, read package.json, install dependencies, run scripts, and distinguish project dependencies from generated node_modules content.

competencies.name: Use Vite development and build workflows
competencies.description: Create, serve, debug, build, preview, and configure a minimal frontend project while understanding bundling, transformation, source maps, and client environment variables conceptually.

competencies.name: Model application data with TypeScript
competencies.description: Use primitive, object, array, union, optional, literal, and reusable types at the boundary where they clarify JavaScript assumptions.

competencies.name: Narrow values and type functions
competencies.description: Type parameters and returns, use control-flow narrowing, and distinguish compile-time checking from runtime validation.

competencies.name: Type browser APIs safely
competencies.description: Handle nullable DOM queries, specific element capabilities, event targets, form data, and reusable generic helpers without unsafe global assertions.

competencies.name: Validate external data at runtime
competencies.description: Treat parsed JSON as untrusted, check required shapes, and produce typed success/failure results for the rest of the application.

competencies.name: Design valuable automated tests
competencies.description: Choose test boundaries, arrange inputs, act, assert observable outcomes, and cover normal, boundary, failure, and regression behavior.

competencies.name: Test DOM behavior from the user perspective
competencies.description: Query by roles and labels, simulate meaningful interactions, await asynchronous outcomes, and avoid coupling tests to private implementation details.

competencies.name: Model interfaces as React components
competencies.description: Divide a design into purposeful components whose boundaries reflect repeated or independently meaningful UI responsibilities.

competencies.name: Render declarative UI with JSX and props
competencies.description: Translate semantic HTML into JSX, pass read-only inputs, compose children, and render data without mutating props.

competencies.name: Model local React state intentionally
competencies.description: Choose the minimal state that changes over time and derive everything else during rendering when possible.

competencies.name: Update React state safely from events
competencies.description: Use event handlers and state setters with immutable object/array updates and functional updates when the next value depends on the previous one.

competencies.name: Build controlled React forms
competencies.description: Connect labels, values, change events, constraints, validation feedback, submission states, and recovery without losing native form behavior.

competencies.name: Choose and lift shared state
competencies.description: Place state at the closest common owner, pass values and handlers explicitly, and avoid contradictory copies across components.

competencies.name: Use React Effects for external synchronization
competencies.description: Distinguish rendering and events from Effects, declare dependencies, clean up subscriptions or requests, and remove Effects that only derive state.

competencies.name: Build resilient React data flows
competencies.description: Coordinate route/prop inputs, request lifecycles, stale results, cached intent, and accessible loading, empty, error, and retry states.

competencies.name: Implement client-side routing
competencies.description: Define route hierarchies, layouts, parameters, navigation, not-found behavior, and direct-load expectations with a maintained React router.

competencies.name: Use URLs as appropriate application state
competencies.description: Represent shareable navigation, path parameters, and search/filter state in URLs while distinguishing it from local or server state.

competencies.name: Extract reusable React logic with custom Hooks
competencies.description: Share stateful synchronization or behavior through Hooks while keeping Hook calls valid, inputs explicit, and component output local.

competencies.name: Choose local, lifted, and contextual state
competencies.description: Distinguish local UI, derived, URL, server, and broadly shared state, then choose the smallest ownership mechanism that fits.

competencies.name: Translate design artifacts into implementation decisions
competencies.description: Inspect spacing, type, tokens, components, states, responsiveness, and missing specifications, then ask bounded clarification questions.

competencies.name: Build accessible React components
competencies.description: Preserve native semantics, keyboard operation, focus, names, states, contrast, motion preferences, and restrained ARIA across reusable components.

competencies.name: Test React components through behavior
competencies.description: Render components with realistic providers, query accessible output, interact as a user, and assert visible outcomes rather than component internals.

competencies.name: Test asynchronous and routed React flows
competencies.description: Control network boundaries, await state transitions, isolate test state, and verify navigation, errors, retries, and accessibility-relevant behavior.

competencies.name: Measure and improve frontend performance
competencies.description: Use network, performance, Lighthouse, and Core Web Vitals evidence to prioritize images, loading, rendering, caching, and bundle improvements.

competencies.name: Apply frontend security boundaries
competencies.description: Avoid unsafe HTML, exposed secrets, token myths, untrusted output, careless dependencies, and authentication/authorization confusion.

competencies.name: Automate critical browser journeys
competencies.description: Use Playwright locators, isolated test data, web-first assertions, cross-browser projects, and traces for a small high-value end-to-end suite.

competencies.name: Deploy and diagnose a frontend application
competencies.description: Configure a free-enough static host, SPA route fallback, HTTPS/domain concepts, environment values, build logs, and rollback-aware verification.

competencies.name: Plan and communicate frontend work
competencies.description: Clarify requirements, identify risks, break scope into tasks, estimate, report progress, document blockers, and negotiate a smaller safe slice when needed.

competencies.name: Collaborate across design and backend boundaries
competencies.description: Resolve design ambiguity and API contract questions with explicit request, response, error, authentication, state, and responsibility decisions.

competencies.name: Frame and architect an independent frontend product
competencies.description: Define users, problem, scope, flows, routes, components, data contracts, states, accessibility, testing, performance, and deployment constraints.

competencies.name: Build a risk-first vertical slice
competencies.description: Implement one thin production path across UI, state, API, validation, tests, and deployment to validate architecture before expanding scope.

competencies.name: Implement a production-style React application independently
competencies.description: Deliver planned routes, components, forms, state, API behavior, and responsive states with explainable architecture and controlled scope.

competencies.name: Operate quality gates during delivery
competencies.description: Use typecheck, lint/format policy, unit/integration/E2E tests, accessibility review, performance measurement, security review, and code review as release evidence.

competencies.name: Release and operate a frontend product
competencies.description: Complete production validation, deployment, smoke monitoring, rollback/redeploy, documentation, and issue triage for a frontend release.

competencies.name: Present and defend frontend engineering evidence
competencies.description: Explain product scope, architecture, trade-offs, accessibility, testing, performance, debugging, collaboration, and limitations using deployed work and source history.

skillCheck.title: Week 1 Understanding Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all ten questions from the assigned Core learning. The required Build separately proves that you can apply the skills.

questions.prompt: A browser requests `/about/index.html`. Which system normally sends the file back?

options.label: The CSS parser inside the page
The text editor that created the file
The web server responsible for that address

questions.explanation: The server handles the request and returns a response; the browser then interprets the returned file.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of HTML in a webpage?

options.label: Describe the content structure and meaning

questions.explanation: HTML communicates structure and semantics; CSS presents it and JavaScript can change behavior.

questions.prompt: A stylesheet exists but the page looks unstyled. What should you inspect first?

options.label: Whether the HTML link points to the actual CSS file path

questions.explanation: A wrong relative path prevents the browser from loading the stylesheet, which the Network panel or page source can reveal.

questions.prompt: Which URL part identifies the protocol used for a request?
questions.explanation: The scheme or protocol appears before `://`; the domain and path identify the destination.

questions.prompt: Why is the browser console useful during a first JavaScript experiment?

options.label: It reports runtime messages and errors produced by the page
It guarantees the HTML is accessible

questions.explanation: The console exposes logged values and JavaScript failures; it is evidence for diagnosis, not a deployment tool.

questions.prompt: A learner double-clicks index.html and sees a `file:` address. What does that show?

options.label: The browser loaded a local file rather than requesting a hosted site
The browser requested the page from a local development server over HTTP
The browser became a web server

questions.explanation: A `file:` URL points to the local filesystem. Hosting later uses an HTTP or HTTPS address.

questions.prompt: What is the clearest evidence that script.js loaded successfully?

options.label: The Network panel lists script.js even though its request returned an error
A deliberate console message or visible interaction from that file occurs

questions.explanation: Observable browser behavior or a loaded Network entry proves execution more reliably than a filename or editor color.

questions.prompt: A button should change text but nothing happens. Which sequence is strongest?

options.label: Reproduce it, inspect console and element wiring, form a hypothesis, then change one cause
Change both the HTML and JavaScript, then refresh to see whether either edit helped

questions.explanation: Controlled diagnosis preserves evidence and tests one explanation at a time.

questions.prompt: Which file organization is easiest for another beginner to inspect?

options.label: A named project folder with index.html, styles.css, and script.js
A project folder containing index.html and one combined file named code.txt

questions.explanation: A predictable folder and conventional entry filename make the relationships inspectable.

questions.prompt: What should a learner be able to explain after the first page works?

options.label: How the editor decides which HTML, CSS, and JavaScript the browser can display
How the browser found each file and what HTML, CSS, and JavaScript contributed
How to operate a production database
Why every site must use React

questions.explanation: The intended mental model is the browser loading coordinated files; frameworks and backend systems are later concerns.

options.label: Use a lower heading level for a larger number

Add several h1 elements until one looks right

questions.prompt: When should an image use empty alternative text?

Use a blockquote and provide the source in an appropriate citation

skillCheck.instructions: Answer all ten questions from the assigned Core learning. The required Build separately proves that you can apply the skills.

questions.prompt: A text input has placeholder text but no label. What is the key problem?

options.label: The placeholder does not provide a persistent, reliable accessible name
The browser converts the input to a button

questions.explanation: A visible label remains available and is associated with the control; placeholder text can disappear and has other usability limits.

questions.prompt: Several radio buttons answer “Preferred contact method.” What should group them?

options.label: One placeholder shared by all controls

questions.explanation: The fieldset groups related controls and the legend supplies the group question.

questions.prompt: A form rejects an email address and only turns the border red. What is missing?

options.label: A clear text error that identifies the field and how to correct it
A warning icon beside the field with its meaning communicated only by color

questions.explanation: Color alone is insufficient; actionable feedback must communicate the problem and recovery.

questions.prompt: When is a table appropriate?

options.label: Whenever two items should sit side by side
Whenever a form has many controls
When information has meaningful row-and-column relationships

questions.explanation: Tables represent data relationships, not general page layout.

questions.prompt: What does a table caption contribute?

options.label: A CSS selector for every cell
A concise name or purpose for the table
A replacement for all header cells
A link to download the data

questions.explanation: A caption helps users identify the table; headers still define row and column relationships.

questions.prompt: Which input type offers browser-aware email semantics?
questions.explanation: The email input type communicates expected data and enables relevant browser behavior, while server validation is still needed.

questions.prompt: Why should a submit button remain a real `button` element?

options.label: It stores the form in localStorage
It supplies built-in keyboard and form behavior

questions.explanation: Native controls provide semantics and interaction behavior that a generic clickable container would need to recreate.

questions.prompt: A required field is empty. Which message is most actionable?

options.label: “Invalid.” at the top with no field reference
“Enter your full name.” beside the Full name field

questions.explanation: Specific, located guidance tells the learner what happened and what action will resolve it.

questions.prompt: What should a keyboard-only form check verify?

options.label: The mouse pointer changes on hover
Every field has a different color
Every control can receive focus, even if its purpose or exit path is unclear
Every interactive control can be reached, understood, operated, and exited in a logical order

questions.explanation: Keyboard testing examines focus order and operability, not visual decoration or framework choice.

questions.prompt: Client-side validation reports success. What remains true?

options.label: The browser has authorized the user
The server must still validate untrusted submitted data
The form no longer needs labels

questions.explanation: Client validation improves feedback but cannot establish server-side trust or persistence.

questions.prompt: Which structure best represents an ordered product collection?

questions.prompt: What does `map` return?

A Boolean for the whole collection
The original array with every item deleted

questions.explanation: `map` performs a one-to-one transformation into a new array.

questions.prompt: Which method best selects all in-stock products?
questions.explanation: `filter` returns every item whose predicate is truthy; `find` returns only the first match.

questions.prompt: Why can `sort` surprise code that reuses the original array?

questions.explanation: Destructuring is concise property access; it does not freeze nested data.

questions.prompt: Two objects contain identical fields but `a === b` is false. Why?

Strict equality checks property order only
Objects compare by reference identity with strict equality
One object must be an array

options.label: The accumulator can become undefined for later iterations
Every object gains a new property

It forces every product to be visible

questions.prompt: Why prefer `textContent` for untrusted task text?

options.label: It inserts text without parsing it as HTML markup

questions.prompt: A form submit reloads the page before JavaScript processes it. What should the handler consider?

options.label: Stop propagation so the browser no longer performs the form element’s default submission

Convert the form to a div

questions.prompt: What information does `event.target` describe?

options.label: The element on which the event originated
Every listener registered in the app

options.label: The state array automatically persists every task and filter choice across browser sessions
Rendering and filtering can derive from one consistent model instead of scattered DOM guesses

questions.prompt: When is event delegation useful?

options.label: When controls have unrelated behaviors but share a visual container that never changes
When a stable ancestor can handle similar events from many dynamic descendants

questions.explanation: Delegation uses propagation to avoid attaching repeated listeners to dynamic items.

questions.prompt: A click handler runs twice after rerendering. What is a likely cause?

options.label: The same listener was attached during multiple renders without a matching cleanup step
Listeners were added repeatedly without removing or avoiding duplicates

questions.explanation: Repeated listener registration produces repeated responses to one event.

A button with an accessible name
A plain span with no keyboard behavior
An image with empty alt text

options.label: Secretly changing the source state while creating the view
Replace the source state with the filtered or sorted version that is currently being rendered

questions.explanation: Rendering should describe the current state; hidden mutation makes outcomes harder to predict.

questions.prompt: How can a propagation bug be investigated?

options.label: Log target/currentTarget and inspect where listeners are registered
Log only the event target, because the target identifies every listener that handled the event

questions.explanation: Event-path evidence shows where an interaction originated and which listener handled it.

questions.prompt: Why is client-side validation not a security boundary?

options.label: A client can be bypassed or modified, so the server must validate submitted data
Browser validation runs before submission, so it protects the server from altered requests

questions.explanation: Client validation improves the experience but cannot establish trust.

questions.prompt: What does `FormData` help collect?
questions.explanation: FormData represents form submissions using control names and values.

questions.prompt: A custom error is shown visually but not associated with its field. What should improve?

options.label: Connect the message through suitable semantics and update accessible state
Move the error beside the field visually without adding a programmatic relationship

questions.prompt: What type does localStorage return for a stored item?
questions.explanation: Structured values require explicit serialization and parsing.

questions.prompt: Which data should not be treated as securely hidden in localStorage?

options.label: Authentication secrets or sensitive personal data
An expiring access token, because browser storage keeps authentication values private

questions.explanation: Page scripts and people with device access may read localStorage; it is not a secure secret vault.

questions.prompt: A stored JSON value is malformed. What should the page do?

options.label: Catch the parse failure, use a safe default, and offer recovery
Ignore the malformed value and keep rendering as though the stored object were complete

questions.explanation: Defensive parsing prevents persistent bad data from trapping the learner.

questions.prompt: How does sessionStorage differ from localStorage at a high level?

options.label: Its data is shared by all tabs for the origin and cleared only when the browser is uninstalled
It is shared by every website
Its data is scoped to the page session/tab and is cleared when that session ends

questions.explanation: Both are origin scoped and string based, but their lifetimes differ.

questions.prompt: Why preserve entered values after validation fails?

options.label: It removes the need for instructions
The learner can correct specific problems without repeating valid work

questions.explanation: Recovery should minimize unnecessary re-entry and keep context.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a storage-key namespace?

options.label: Reduce collisions by giving related application data a deliberate name
Convert each stored string into an object before assigning it a short generic storage key

questions.explanation: Clear key design makes ownership and reset behavior predictable.

The page title is too long

questions.prompt: What does an HTTP 404 response normally mean?

options.label: The JavaScript file has a syntax error
The server could not find the requested resource
The browser is offline in every case

questions.explanation: A 404 is an HTTP response status describing the requested resource.

questions.prompt: Why can fetch resolve even when the server returns 500?

options.label: Fetch rejects only for 500 responses, while successful HTTP statuses return Response objects
Fetch rejects for certain request/network failures, while HTTP error statuses still produce Response objects

questions.explanation: Code must inspect `response.ok` or status before treating the exchange as successful.

questions.prompt: What does `await response.json()` do?

options.label: Asynchronously reads the response body and parses JSON
Validates every property against a schema

questions.explanation: Parsing produces JavaScript data but does not guarantee the expected application shape.

questions.prompt: A request remains pending. Which UI state should be visible?

options.label: A clear loading state that does not imply success
The previous error as permanent truth
No feedback while controls repeatedly submit

questions.explanation: Pending work is a real state and should prevent misleading or duplicate behavior.

questions.prompt: A successful response contains an empty array. What should the interface show?

options.label: Keep the loading state visible because an empty array means the request has not finished
An intentional empty state explaining that no results matched

questions.explanation: Empty is a valid success outcome, distinct from failure or pending.

questions.prompt: What is JSON?

options.label: A text data format commonly exchanged between clients and servers
A JavaScript object stored directly in memory and shared securely with a remote database

questions.explanation: JSON encodes data; the application still decides how to validate and use it.

questions.prompt: Where can a frontend engineer inspect response status and body timing?
questions.explanation: Network tools expose requests, statuses, headers, timing, and response content.

questions.prompt: A rapid second search finishes before the first. What risk exists?

options.label: The server converts GET to CSS
The array loses all object fields
The browser removes the form label
The older response may overwrite the newer intended result

questions.explanation: Out-of-order async completion can produce stale UI unless requests are cancelled, ignored, or associated with current intent.

questions.prompt: What information belongs in an API contract discussion?

options.label: Request inputs, response shapes, statuses, validation errors, and authentication expectations
The response shape and successful status only; clients can infer errors and authentication later

questions.explanation: The contract defines how frontend and backend behavior meet.

questions.prompt: A retry button immediately starts many overlapping requests when clicked repeatedly. What should improve?

options.label: Start every request and display whichever response completes first, regardless of current intent
Track pending state and prevent or coordinate duplicate submissions

questions.explanation: Submission controls should reflect the current request lifecycle.

questions.prompt: What should happen before changing code for a reported bug?

options.label: Reproduce it reliably and capture the conditions
Read the suspected function and change the most likely line before reproducing the report

questions.explanation: A reliable reproduction creates a baseline for diagnosis and verification.

questions.prompt: What does a stack trace help reveal?

options.label: The call path leading to the thrown error

questions.explanation: Stack frames show how execution reached the failure.

questions.prompt: Why pause at a breakpoint just before the failure?

options.label: Confirm that execution reached the function, then continue without inspecting current values
Inspect current values and execution state before the symptom changes them

questions.explanation: Breakpoints expose local variables, scope, and control flow at a chosen moment.

questions.prompt: A catch block is empty. What is the main risk?

options.label: The failure becomes invisible and the program may continue with invalid state
The browser supplies a generic message, so the application may safely continue with prior state

questions.explanation: Handling means recovery, transformation, or useful reporting—not silence.

questions.prompt: When is throwing an Error appropriate?

options.label: When the function cannot fulfill its contract and the caller needs a failure signal
Whenever input is imperfect, even when the function can return an expected validation result

questions.explanation: A thrown error communicates exceptional failure through the call chain.

questions.prompt: A layout bug disappears when content is shortened. What hypothesis is strongest?

options.label: The event handler is registered twice, causing the browser to duplicate the layout content
An intrinsic sizing, wrapping, or overflow constraint is involved

questions.explanation: The content-dependent reproduction points to layout constraints.

questions.prompt: The Network panel shows 401. What category should be investigated?

options.label: The response body could not be destructured, so JavaScript converted the status to 401

questions.explanation: A 401 is response evidence about authentication, not a rendering algorithm.

questions.prompt: Why change one suspected cause at a time?

options.label: It preserves the ability to connect the observed result to a specific hypothesis
Several simultaneous changes make it faster to identify which hypothesis repaired the failure
CSS files cannot contain several rules

questions.explanation: Controlled experiments produce stronger causal evidence.

questions.prompt: What makes a regression check valuable?

options.label: It confirms the page currently works, even if it does not exercise the original failure conditions
It proves the original failure stays repaired under its known conditions

questions.explanation: A repeatable check protects the behavior that was broken.

questions.prompt: A fix removes the error but deletes required behavior. Is it complete?

options.label: Yes; absence of a console error is sufficient
No; the original requirement and surrounding behavior must still pass
Yes; smaller output is always correct
No; every fix must add a dependency

questions.explanation: A repair must satisfy the intended behavior, not merely suppress the symptom.

It is the browser rendering engine

questions.prompt: What does package.json record?

The exact installed package source and complete node_modules contents for the current computer

questions.prompt: What does TypeScript primarily add to JavaScript?

Static analysis of value relationships before runtime

questions.prompt: When is type inference usually sufficient?

When an initializer or return expression makes the intended type clear
When a value crosses a network boundary, because inference also validates its runtime shape

The value is a CSS union

It converts every value to text
It validates a server response completely

questions.explanation: Control-flow analysis refines the union based on the runtime check.

questions.prompt: What is an optional object property?

options.label: A property the compiler removes from the object whenever a caller does not read it
A property that may be absent and therefore must be handled accordingly
A property stored only on servers
A property that cannot have a type

questions.explanation: Optional syntax models possible absence rather than removing checks.

questions.prompt: Why avoid broad `any`?

options.label: It turns off useful checking and lets unsafe assumptions spread

questions.explanation: `any` is an escape hatch; `unknown` plus narrowing is safer for uncertain input.

questions.prompt: An API value is typed by assertion without checking it. What remains risky?

options.label: The browser will reject JSON syntax
Runtime data may not match the asserted shape

questions.explanation: Assertions tell the checker what to believe; they do not verify data.

questions.prompt: When do a type alias and interface both work well?

options.label: For naming a common object shape used across code

questions.explanation: Both can model object structures; the choice should serve project conventions and required features.

questions.prompt: What does a typed function return annotation make inspectable?

options.label: The result contract promised to callers

questions.explanation: A return type can catch missing or inconsistent outcomes.

questions.prompt: A compiler error reveals a possible undefined value. What is the strongest response?

options.label: Assert the value is defined so the compiler accepts the code without changing runtime behavior
Handle the legitimate absent case or correct the data model

questions.explanation: The error exposes an assumption; repair should reflect real behavior.

Open docs, close browser, delete output

It works only for CSS classes

When the element should appear asynchronously after an action
When testing a pure number function

questions.prompt: What should happen after the test suite passes?

A value computed from current props or state for rendering

questions.prompt: Why implement focus styles from the beginning?

options.label: Keyboard users need a visible indication of the active control

questions.explanation: Focus visibility is core interaction feedback, not late decoration.

questions.explanation: Zoom testing reveals fixed-size and overflow assumptions.

What a user can perceive or do through the rendered interface

options.label: The network boundary or service contract, not every child component

questions.prompt: Why isolate test storage and state?

React forbids multiple renders in one test, so shared storage should preserve the first render

questions.prompt: Why include keyboard behavior in component tests?

It protects interaction semantics that pointer-only checks can miss

questions.explanation: The suite must be sensitive to broken contracts and tolerant of sound internal change.

Measure a representative experience and identify the actual bottleneck

questions.explanation: Baseline evidence prevents premature or irrelevant work.

questions.prompt: What does Largest Contentful Paint describe?

options.label: When the largest visible content element is rendered in the viewport
How long the application’s TypeScript takes to compile before the browser receives any content

questions.explanation: LCP is a user-centric loading metric and needs contextual measurement.

questions.prompt: Why resize and encode images appropriately?

options.label: Oversized assets waste transfer and decode work for the rendered need
Large source images cannot be styled responsively, so CSS rejects them before rendering

questions.explanation: Image bytes often dominate page weight and should match display requirements.

questions.prompt: When is code splitting useful?

options.label: When a meaningful feature or route can load later instead of burdening initial use
For every small function, because separate chunks always reduce the initial network cost

questions.explanation: Splitting has request and complexity costs, so use measured, meaningful boundaries.

questions.prompt: Why is `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` named as a warning?

options.label: Untrusted HTML can create an XSS path if not correctly sanitized
It prevents React from rendering any HTML string, including content created by the application

questions.prompt: Can a frontend environment variable safely hide an API secret?

options.label: Yes, if its name starts with VITE

questions.explanation: Frontend code and traffic are observable; secrets require a trusted server boundary.

questions.prompt: What is the distinction between authentication and authorization?

options.label: Authentication identifies a subject; authorization decides permitted actions
Authentication encrypts the application bundle; authorization compresses it for permitted users

questions.explanation: A logged-in user still needs server-enforced permission checks.

questions.prompt: Why review dependency health before adding a package?

options.label: Browsers reject packages with many dependencies before the production bundle can execute
It introduces code, maintenance, size, and supply-chain risk

questions.explanation: A dependency decision should be proportionate to the capability it adds.

questions.prompt: A Lighthouse score improves after disabling an essential feature. Is that a valid win?

options.label: Yes; the score is the only requirement
No; performance improvements must preserve required user behavior

questions.explanation: Metrics guide product work but do not replace functional requirements.

questions.prompt: What should production-preview verification include?

options.label: Primary flows, direct routes, assets, errors, and console/network behavior from the built output

questions.explanation: The deployable artifact can differ from development and needs its own smoke check.
